t: Section 4002 of the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2008 (26 U.S.C. 3304 note) is amended by adding at the end the following:“(c) Special Rule.—“(1) In general.—If, at the time that the amount established in an individual’s account under subsection (b)(1) is exhausted or at any time thereafter, such individual’s State is in an extended benefit period (as determined under paragraph (2)), such account shall be augmented by an amount equal to the lesser of—“(A) 50 percent of the total amount of regular compensation (including dependents’ allowances) payable to the individual during the individual’s benefit year under the State law, or“(B) 13 times the individual’s average weekly benefit amount (as determined under subsection (b)(2)) for the benefit year.“(2) Extended benefit period.—For purposes of paragraph (1), a State shall be considered to be in an extended benefit period, as of any given time, if—“(A) such a period is then in effect for such State under the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970;“(B) such a period would then be in effect for such State under such Act if section 203(d) of such Act—“(i) were applied by substituting ‘4’ for ‘5’ each place it appears; and“(ii) did not include the requirement under paragraph (1)(A) thereof; or“(C) such a period would then be in effect for such State under such Act if—“(i) section 203(f) of such Act were applied to such State (regardless of whether the State by law had provided for such application); and“(ii) such section 203(f)—“(I) were applied by substituting ‘6.0’ for ‘6.5’ in paragraph (1)(A)(i) thereof; and“(II) did not include the requirement under paragraph (1)(A)(ii) thereof.“(3) Limitation.—The account of an individual may be augmented not more than once under this subsection.”.

fable.w: This section only sets a formula for augmenting an individual's emergency unemployment compensation account and defines when a State is treated as being in an extended benefit period. The tempting reading is that the references to States and State law signal federal-state coordination, but the State's status is fixed mechanically by statutory triggers, with no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue. It is a benefit-calculation provision, and no outside party takes part in any federal decision.

opus.w: This section sets a formula that adds to an individual's emergency unemployment compensation account when the state's unemployment conditions meet set thresholds. States show up only as the place whose statistics trigger the extra benefit, not as parties consulted on a federal decision. Benefit eligibility and amounts are not participation, and the section creates no hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body or right to sue.

opus.b: 1. **Thinking:** The tempting reading is that the section involves states, because it keeps referring to "such individual's State" and to the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act. That reading fails. The state's "extended benefit period" status is only a mechanical trigger, calculated by formula, that decides whether a person's emergency unemployment benefit account gets topped up. No state, member of the public or other outside party is consulted before any federal decision. The section is about how much benefit an individual receives, and benefits fall outside the definition. There is also no hearing, comment period, rulemaking authority, advisory body or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes a formula for augmenting unemployment benefit accounts based on specific conditions (e.g., whether a state is in an extended benefit period). It does not require the federal government to consult with states, individuals, or other outside parties before making a decision. The process is automatic and mathematical, lacking any element of advisory input, public comment, or coordination with outside entities regarding a discretionary federal action.

qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the statute involves "States" and "individuals," it implies some form of consultation or coordination. However, the text strictly defines mathematical formulas for calculating benefit amounts based on existing legal statuses (e.g., whether a state is in an extended benefit period). It does not require the federal government to consult with states or individuals before making a decision; it merely sets the rules for how benefits are calculated. The interaction is purely administrative and formulaic, not participatory in the sense of advisory input or coordination before a discretionary decision.
